decks.title: Trial Balance — Part 1: Meaning, Objectives, Advantages and Limitations
goals: State the meaning of a trial balance and its objectives and advantages
Explain why equal totals do not prove that the accounts are free from errors, and name the errors that leave the totals equal
Distinguish the errors that disturb the trial balance from those that do not

slides.heading: The trial balance: a check before the final accounts
slides.body_md: Part 1: what a **trial balance** is, what it is meant to do, and why agreeing totals do **not** prove the books are error free.

nodes.label: Transactions in the books of original entry

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: transactions are recorded, posted to the ledger and balanced, the balances are listed in the trial balance, and the trial balance leads to the final accounts
visual.caption: Where the trial balance stands

slides.narration: Welcome. Once all transactions are posted and every ledger account is balanced, the accountant lists the balances in one statement called the trial balance. In this part we see what it is, what it checks, and why equal totals are comforting but never a proof.

slides.heading: Meaning of a trial balance
bullets: A **trial balance** is a **statement** of the balances of all ledger accounts on a given date.
Debit balances go in one column and credit balances in the other.
If the posting is arithmetically accurate, **the two totals agree**.

rows: It has no folio and is not a part of the double entry
Usually the last day of the year; some firms prepare it every month
Closing balances of all ledger accounts, with debit balances in one column and credit balances in the other
The two columns are added, and they should come to the same figure

visual.alt: Table of four features of a trial balance: it is a statement and not an account, it is made on a date, it lists ledger balances in a debit and a credit column, and its two totals should agree

slides.narration: A trial balance is a statement, not an account. It lists the closing balance of every ledger account on a date, with debit balances in one column and credit balances in the other. Because every transaction has equal debits and credits, the two totals should be equal.

slides.heading: Objectives of a trial balance
slides.body_md: The main objective is to test **arithmetical accuracy**; it also gives a **summary of the ledger** and the **base for the final accounts**.

headers: How the trial balance serves it
rows: If every transaction has equal debit and credit, the two columns agree
All the balances are seen together on a single page
The trading and profit and loss accounts and the balance sheet are drawn from it
A difference in the totals warns that something is wrong before the final accounts are made

visual.alt: Table of four objectives of a trial balance: checking arithmetical accuracy, giving one summary of the ledger, providing the base for the final accounts and helping to locate mistakes

slides.narration: A trial balance has four uses. It tests the arithmetical accuracy of the books. It gives one summary of all the ledger balances. It is the base from which the final accounts are drawn. And a difference in the totals warns the accountant to look for mistakes before going further.

slides.heading: Which side does each balance take?
slides.body_md: Assets, expenses, losses, purchases, sales return, opening stock and drawings stand on the **debit** side. Capital, liabilities, incomes, sales, purchases return and provisions stand on the **credit** side.

rows: Assets: cash, bank, debtors, furniture, machinery

visual.alt: Table of the kinds of balance that stand on the debit side of a trial balance and on the credit side: assets, expenses, purchases, sales return, opening stock and drawings on the debit side; capital, liabilities, incomes, sales, purchases return and provisions on the credit side
visual.caption: Which side does each balance take

slides.narration: Before listing balances, remember the sides. Assets, expenses, losses, purchases, sales return, opening stock and drawings are debit balances. Capital, liabilities, incomes, sales, purchases return and provisions are credit balances. This one table settles most questions.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a trial balance from ledger balances
slides.body_md: **Kasaragod Spice Traders**, an imagined firm, has the ledger balances shown below on 31 March 2028. Prepare the trial balance.
bullets: Debit balances total ₹11,05,500.
Credit balances (sales, creditors, capital) also total ₹11,05,500, so the totals agree.

visual.alt: Trial balance of Kasaragod Spice Traders, an imagined firm, on 31 March 2028: thirteen balances, with each of the two columns totalling eleven lakh five thousand five hundred rupees
visual.caption: Trial balance of Kasaragod Spice Traders on 31 March 2028

slides.narration: Each ledger balance is entered once, on the side of its nature. Cash, bank, debtors, furniture, machinery, purchases, wages, rent, salaries and drawings go to the debit column. Sales, creditors and capital go to the credit column. Each column adds up to rupees eleven lakh five thousand five hundred, so the trial balance agrees.

slides.heading: Quick check: what agreement shows
slides.body_md: Decide what equal totals really prove.
slides.narration: A trial balance agrees. What can the accountant say with certainty? Read the options carefully, and remember that agreement checks only the equality of debit and credit totals.

slides.heading: Advantages of a trial balance
bullets: It gives a **quick check** on the posting of the ledger.
It puts all balances in **one summary**.
It makes the **final accounts easier** to prepare.

rows: Equal totals show that debits and credits have been matched
Every ledger balance can be read from one statement
The figures are picked from one list, in a ready order
A difference tells the accountant to search before going further

visual.alt: Table of four advantages of a trial balance: a quick check on posting, a single summary, easier final accounts and saving time in finding mistakes

slides.narration: The trial balance is useful in four ways. It checks the posting quickly. It gathers every ledger balance in one place. It makes the final accounts easier, because the figures are ready. And it saves time, since a difference tells the accountant to look for a mistake right away.

slides.heading: What agreement of the totals does and does not show
slides.body_md: Equal totals mean that **debits equal credits in the ledger**. They do **not** mean that every transaction was recorded, or that it was entered in the right account.

rows: Debits and credits in the ledger are equal in total
That every transaction has been recorded
The arithmetic of the posting and balancing is probably right
That every entry is in the right account
The books are ready for the final accounts
That the accounting principles have been followed
That errors on the two sides have not cancelled

visual.alt: Table of what agreement of the trial balance shows (equal debits and credits and arithmetical accuracy) and what it does not show (completeness, correct accounts, correct principles and the absence of cancelling errors)

slides.narration: Equal totals show that the debit and credit balances are equal. They do not show that every transaction was recorded, that each entry sits in the right account, that the right principle was followed, or that two mistakes have not cancelled each other. So agreement is a good sign, not a proof.

slides.heading: Errors that the trial balance does not reveal
bullets: **Omission:** a transaction is left out of the books.
**Principle:** the wrong class of account is used.
**Commission:** the wrong account, or a wrong amount on both sides.
**Compensating:** two mistakes cancel each other.

rows: A transaction is left out of the books altogether, so both its debit and credit are missing
Credit sale of ₹22,000 to Tamil Stores is never entered
An entry is made in the wrong class of account, against an accounting principle
Computer bought for ₹36,000 is debited to Purchases A/c
The right principle is followed but the wrong account is used, or the amount is wrong on both sides
Payment of ₹15,000 to Ellora Foods is debited to Sundar Nuts Co.
Two or more mistakes whose effects on the totals cancel each other
Rent debited ₹9,000 too much and commission credited ₹9,000 too much

visual.alt: Table of four errors that do not disturb the trial balance: omission, principle, commission and compensating errors, each with its meaning and an example from Padmini Dry Fruits, an imagined firm

slides.narration: Four kinds of error leave the totals equal. In an error of omission the transaction is not recorded at all. In an error of principle the entry goes to the wrong class of account. In an error of commission the wrong account is used, with the right amount on both sides. Compensating errors cancel each other. Here we only name them. Rectifying them comes later.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: four errors, equal totals
slides.body_md: **Padmini Dry Fruits**, an imagined firm, has correct books with trial balance totals of ₹5,50,000. Four different errors are made, one at a time. Find the effect on the trial balance.
bullets: Omission: Tamil Stores and Sales are both ₹22,000 short.
Principle: Purchases ₹36,000 too high; Computer missing.
Commission: Sundar Nuts Co. is debited instead of Ellora Foods.
Compensating: Rent and Commission received each ₹9,000 too high.

rows: Payment debited to the wrong creditor
Rent and commission wrong by equal amounts

visual.alt: Table for Padmini Dry Fruits: the correct trial balance totals five lakh fifty thousand rupees and four kinds of error leave the two totals equal, although several account balances are wrong
visual.caption: Four errors, and the totals still agree

slides.narration: In the correct books the trial balance totals rupees five lakh fifty thousand. When a credit sale is omitted, both totals fall together. When the computer is debited to purchases, the totals do not change at all. A payment debited to the wrong creditor changes no total. Rent and commission each wrong by the same amount cancel. The trial balance agrees every time.

slides.heading: An error of principle: the totals do not notice
slides.body_md: The computer was bought for cash, so Computer A/c should be debited. It was debited to **Purchases A/c**. Debit and credit are still equal, but two balances are wrong.

visual.alt: Table of the two accounts affected by the computer wrongly debited to Purchases: Computer shows nothing instead of thirty-six thousand rupees, and Purchases is thirty-six thousand rupees too high

slides.narration: In an error of principle, the debit is placed in a wrong class of account, such as a capital item treated as an expense. The credit to cash is correct. The debit total is the same as before. Yet purchases is too high and the computer account shows nothing. The trial balance cannot see this.

slides.heading: Quick check: compensating errors
slides.body_md: True or false?
slides.narration: Read the statement about compensating errors. Think about what must happen to the two totals for such errors to stay hidden.

slides.heading: Compensating errors
slides.body_md: Two or more mistakes, usually on **opposite sides**, whose effects on the totals cancel. Each account is wrong, yet the trial balance agrees.

visual.alt: Table of the two accounts affected by the compensating errors: Rent is nine thousand rupees too high on the debit side and Commission received is nine thousand rupees too high on the credit side

slides.narration: Compensating errors are mistakes that cancel each other. Here rent is debited nine thousand rupees too much, and commission received is credited nine thousand rupees too much. The debit total and the credit total both rise by the same amount, so the trial balance still agrees. The mistakes are independent and happen to be of equal size.

slides.heading: Errors that do disturb the trial balance
bullets: An amount posted on **one side only**.
Different amounts posted on the **debit and credit** sides.
An amount posted twice on the same side, or to the **wrong side**.
An error in **adding** an account or the trial balance.

rows: Credit to a customer left out

visual.alt: Table of four posting errors of Padmini Dry Fruits that make the trial balance disagree, with the debit total, credit total, the side that is higher and the difference
visual.caption: Errors that make the totals differ

slides.narration: These errors upset the equality of debit and credit. One side may be left out, the amounts on the two sides may differ, an amount may be posted twice on the same side, or a column may be added wrongly. The difference between the totals tells us the size of the error, and the higher side tells us where to look.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: finding the difference
slides.body_md: Take the books of Padmini Dry Fruits again. The receipt of ₹60,000 from Tamil Stores is debited to Cash but **never credited** to Tamil Stores. Find the effect on the trial balance.
bullets: Debit total ₹6,10,000; credit total ₹5,50,000.
The debit side is higher by ₹60,000, the amount of the missing credit.

visual.alt: Table of the account affected when the receipt of sixty thousand rupees is debited to Cash but not credited to Tamil Stores: Tamil Stores shows a debit balance sixty thousand rupees too high

slides.narration: The cash receipt is debited but the credit to Tamil Stores is left out. The debit total becomes rupees six lakh ten thousand and the credit total rupees five lakh fifty thousand. The debit side is higher by rupees sixty thousand, exactly the amount of the missing credit. The disagreement warns the accountant that an error exists.

slides.heading: Quick check: the size of the gap
slides.body_md: Complete the sentence.
slides.narration: A one-sided posting leaves the two totals different. Think about which total is larger and by how much, and then fill in the blanks.

slides.heading: Limitations of a trial balance
bullets: Equal totals are **not proof** of accuracy.
Errors of **omission, principle, commission and compensation** stay hidden.
It checks only the **ledger**, not the original records.

rows: Errors that do not disturb the totals stay hidden
Omission, principle, commission and compensating errors pass through
A balance may sit in the wrong account without any difference
Depends on correct posting and balancing
It checks the ledger, not the quality of the original records

visual.alt: Table of four limitations of a trial balance: equal totals are not proof of accuracy, some errors are never shown, wrong accounts can carry right totals, and it checks only the ledger

slides.narration: The trial balance has real limits. Equal totals are not a proof. Four kinds of error go through unnoticed. A balance may sit in the wrong account without any difference. And the trial balance checks the ledger only, not the quality of the original records. The final accounts made from it can therefore still be wrong.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: A statement of ledger balances on a date, debit column and credit column
Arithmetical accuracy, a summary of the ledger, the base for final accounts
Quick check, single summary, easier final accounts
One-sided posting, unequal amounts, wrong side, wrong totals
Agreement is not proof that the books are free from errors

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: meaning, objectives, advantages, the errors a trial balance does not show, the errors it shows and its main limitation

slides.narration: To sum up. A trial balance is a statement of ledger balances on a date. It tests arithmetical accuracy, summarises the ledger and prepares the way for the final accounts. Omission, principle, commission and compensating errors do not disturb it. One-sided posting and unequal amounts do. Agreement is never a proof.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Define the trial balance as a **statement of balances**, not an account.
When asked why agreement is not proof, **name the errors** that leave totals equal and give a one-line example of each.
Do not call omission, principle, commission and compensating errors errors that the trial balance shows; they are the ones it **does not show**.
Mention both **advantages and limitations** when the question has two parts.
slides.narration: In the examination, define the trial balance as a statement and not an account. When asked why agreement is not proof, name the errors that leave the totals equal and give a short example of each. Keep advantages and limitations separate in your answer. Remember that rectification of errors is a separate chapter.

decks.title: Trial Balance — Part 2: Preparing the Trial Balance by the Balance Method
goals: Decide the side of each balance from the nature of the account, including opening stock, closing stock and returns
Find a missing capital as the balancing figure
Prepare ledger accounts from a short set of transactions and then the trial balance

slides.heading: Preparing a trial balance by the balance method
slides.body_md: Part 2: reading ledger balances, placing each on the **correct side**, finding a **missing capital** and building the trial balance from **transactions**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: start from ledger balances, decide the side of each, find a missing capital and build a trial balance from transactions
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Here we prepare trial balances. We use the balance method, in which every ledger account contributes one balance, on one side. We decide the side from the nature of the account, find a missing capital, and start from transactions.

slides.heading: The balance method
bullets: Take the **closing balance** of every ledger account, the balance carried down.
Enter a **debit balance** in the debit column and a **credit balance** in the credit column.
Each account appears **once**; then add both columns.

nodes.label: Decide the side from the nature of the account
Write it in the debit or credit column

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: list the ledger accounts, read each balance carried down, decide its side from its nature, write it in the debit or credit column, and total and compare the two columns
visual.caption: The balance method in five steps

slides.narration: In the balance method each account appears once, with only its closing balance. A debit balance goes to the debit column and a credit balance to the credit column. Then both columns are added and compared. The method is quick, and the final accounts are drawn from the same balances.

slides.heading: Side of each kind of account
slides.body_md: When a list of balances is given **without sides**, decide each side from the **nature** of the account.

rows: Cash, bank, debtors, furniture, land, bills receivable
Wages, rent, salaries, discount allowed, bad debts
Trading items on the debit side
Purchases, sales return, carriage inwards, opening stock
Cash or goods taken by the owner
Capital, creditors, bills payable, loans, bank overdraft
Commission received, discount received, interest received
Trading items on the credit side

visual.alt: Table of eight kinds of ledger account with the side each takes in the trial balance and examples: assets, expenses, trading items on either side, drawings, capital and liabilities, incomes, and provisions
visual.caption: Side of each kind of account

slides.narration: When balances are given without sides, ask what kind of account each one is. Assets, expenses, losses, purchases, sales return, opening stock and drawings are debit balances. Capital, liabilities, incomes, sales, purchases return and provisions are credit balances.

slides.heading: Items that cause confusion
slides.body_md: Opening stock is a **debit** balance. **Closing stock** is found at the year end and is **not in the trial balance** unless it is already entered in the books.

rows: A balance of the last year brought forward in the books
Found at the year end; it goes to the trading account and the balance sheet
Goods come back, so it reduces the sales
Goods go back, so it reduces the purchases
It reduces the owner's capital but is kept in its own account
An amount set aside against possible bad debts, not an asset

visual.alt: Table of eight items that students often place wrongly: opening stock on the debit side, closing stock not entered, sales return on the debit side, purchases return on the credit side, drawings on the debit side, bank overdraft on the credit side, provision on the credit side, and discounts
visual.caption: Items that cause confusion

slides.narration: Some items cause trouble. Opening stock is a debit balance. Closing stock is found at the year end and goes to the trading account and the balance sheet, not the trial balance. Sales return is a debit and purchases return is a credit. Drawings are debit. Bank overdraft and provisions are credit.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: deciding the side of each balance
slides.body_md: **Wardha Hosiery**, an imagined firm, lists these balances on 31 March 2028 without sides. Closing stock of ₹74,000 is given as additional information. Classify each balance and prepare the trial balance.
bullets: Twenty balances go to the trial balance; the **closing stock is left out**.
The debit and credit totals are each ₹12,18,000.

visual.alt: Twenty-one balances of Wardha Hosiery, an imagined firm, on 31 March 2028, each with its nature and its side: twenty go to the trial balance and the closing stock of seventy four thousand rupees is given outside the books and is not entered
visual.caption: Wardha Hosiery: deciding the side of each balance

slides.narration: The first step is to decide the nature of each balance. Opening stock, purchases, sales return, carriage inwards, wages, salaries, bad debts, discount allowed, debtors, plant, drawings and cash are debit balances. The rest, including provision for doubtful debts, bank overdraft and bills payable, are credit balances. Closing stock is given outside the books, so it is not entered.

slides.heading: Worked example 1 continued: the trial balance
slides.body_md: Entering each balance on its side gives the statement below.

visual.alt: Trial balance of Wardha Hosiery on 31 March 2028 with each column totalling twelve lakh eighteen thousand rupees, without the closing stock
visual.caption: Trial balance of Wardha Hosiery

slides.narration: With every balance placed, the trial balance of Wardha Hosiery is ready. Both columns total rupees twelve lakh eighteen thousand. The closing stock does not appear. If it had been entered, the totals would no longer agree, because it would have no matching balance.

slides.heading: Quick check: opening stock
slides.body_md: Choose the side of the opening stock.
slides.narration: A list of balances includes opening stock. Decide whether it goes in the debit column or the credit column, and remember that it is the stock with which the year began.

slides.heading: Reading the side from a ledger account
slides.body_md: The balance carried down is written on the **lighter** side. A balance c/d on the **credit** side is a **debit balance**; a balance c/d on the **debit** side is a **credit balance**.

rows: By Balance c/d on the credit side
To Balance c/d on the debit side

visual.alt: Table of two ledger accounts: a debtor whose debit side is larger, so the balance carried down is written on the credit side and is a debit balance, and a creditor whose credit side is larger, so the balance carried down is on the debit side and is a credit balance
visual.caption: The side of the c/d is the opposite of the nature of the balance

slides.narration: In a ledger account the balance carried down is written on the side that is smaller before balancing. So a balance carried down on the credit side means the debit side was larger, and the account has a debit balance. A balance carried down on the debit side means a credit balance. The trial balance takes the nature, not the side of the carried down line.

slides.heading: A missing capital
slides.body_md: If every balance except capital is given and the trial balance must agree, **capital is the balancing figure**: debit balances minus the other credit balances.

rows: 1. Add all debit balances other than capital
Total of the debit column without capital
2. Add all credit balances other than capital
Total of the credit column without capital
Debits minus credits of the other balances
4. Enter the capital on the credit side

visual.alt: Table of four steps to find a missing capital: add the debit balances, add the credit balances other than capital, take the difference as capital, and enter it on the credit side

slides.narration: Sometimes the capital is not given. The totals must still agree, so capital is the balancing figure. Add the debit balances. Add the credit balances other than capital. The difference is the capital, and it goes to the credit side.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: finding the capital
slides.body_md: **Rohtak Sports Mart**, an imagined firm, gives these balances on 31 March 2028 without the capital. Find the capital and prepare the trial balance.
bullets: Debit balances ₹11,57,000; other credit balances ₹7,12,000.

rows: Total of credit balances other than capital

visual.alt: Working for the capital of Rohtak Sports Mart, an imagined firm: debit balances of eleven lakh fifty seven thousand rupees less other credit balances of seven lakh twelve thousand rupees leave four lakh forty five thousand rupees as capital
visual.caption: Missing capital of Rohtak Sports Mart

slides.narration: The debit balances total rupees eleven lakh fifty seven thousand. The credit balances other than capital total rupees seven lakh twelve thousand. The difference of rupees four lakh forty five thousand is the capital and goes to the credit side. Now both columns total rupees eleven lakh fifty seven thousand.

slides.heading: Worked example 2 continued: the trial balance
slides.body_md: Now the trial balance with the capital entered on the credit side.

visual.alt: Trial balance of Rohtak Sports Mart with the capital of four lakh forty five thousand rupees found as the balancing figure, each column totalling eleven lakh fifty seven thousand rupees
visual.caption: Trial balance after finding the capital

slides.narration: With the capital of rupees four lakh forty five thousand entered, both columns agree at rupees eleven lakh fifty seven thousand. Note that the agreement is forced by the method. It does not check the figures given, which is why a missing capital is found only when the other balances are trusted.

slides.heading: Quick check: missing capital
slides.body_md: Find the balancing figure.
slides.narration: A list gives the debit balances and the credit balances other than capital. Add each group, take the difference, and say what the capital must be for the trial balance to agree.

slides.heading: From transactions to a trial balance
bullets: Pass a **journal entry** for every transaction.
Post to the ledger accounts, then **balance each one**.
List the balances and total the two columns.

visual.alt: Route map of the third example: analyse each transaction, pass the journal entries, post them to the ledger accounts, balance every account and prepare the trial balance
visual.caption: From transactions to a trial balance

slides.narration: When transactions are given, work in order. Analyse each transaction and pass a journal entry. Post the entries to the ledger accounts. Balance every account. List the balances in a trial balance. The totals of the debit and credit sides of all the ledger accounts are also equal, which gives a second check.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: transactions of Palampur Woollens
slides.body_md: **Palampur Woollens**, an imagined firm, has ten transactions in January 2028. Analyse them, post them and prepare the trial balance as on 31 January 2028.

rows: Business started with cash and furniture
Cash paid to Gill Wool Mills

visual.alt: Ten transactions of Palampur Woollens, an imagined firm, in January 2028, each with the accounts debited and credited and the amount
visual.caption: Transactions of Palampur Woollens, January 2028

slides.narration: First analyse each transaction. The business starts with cash and furniture, which is capital. Purchases and sales are made for cash and on credit. Rent, salaries and a withdrawal by the proprietor are paid in cash. Money is received from one customer and paid to one supplier.

slides.heading: Worked example 3 continued: the ledger
slides.body_md: Post each entry. The **Cash account** has ₹2,90,000 on the debit side and ₹1,47,000 on the credit side, so the balance carried down is ₹1,43,000.

visual.alt: Cash account of Palampur Woollens for January 2028: receipts on the debit side, payments on the credit side, and a balance of one lakh forty three thousand rupees carried down
visual.caption: Cash account of Palampur Woollens

slides.narration: Each entry is posted to two accounts. The cash account receives the capital, the cash sale and the collection from the customer on the debit side. It pays for purchases, rent, the supplier, salaries and drawings on the credit side. Debits exceed credits, so rupees one lakh forty three thousand is carried down as a debit balance.

slides.heading: Worked example 3 continued: balances and trial balance
slides.body_md: The other nine accounts are balanced in the same way. Their totals and balances are below; the trial balance follows.

visual.alt: Table of the ten ledger accounts of Palampur Woollens after posting, each with its debit total, credit total, balance and the side of the balance
visual.caption: Balances of all the ledger accounts

slides.narration: After posting, the debit and credit totals of every ledger account are known. The balance is the difference. Cash, furniture, purchases, debtor, rent, salaries and drawings have debit balances. Capital, the supplier and sales have credit balances.

slides.heading: Worked example 3 concluded: the trial balance
slides.body_md: Each balance is written once on its side. The totals agree at ₹3,80,000.

visual.alt: Trial balance of Palampur Woollens on 31 January 2028: ten balances, with each column totalling three lakh eighty thousand rupees
visual.caption: Trial balance of Palampur Woollens

slides.narration: The trial balance of Palampur Woollens has ten lines. The debit column and the credit column both come to rupees three lakh eighty thousand. As all entries were correct and complete, the trial balance agrees, and the accountant may go on to the final accounts.

slides.heading: Quick check: balance carried down
slides.body_md: Read the account.
slides.narration: A ledger account is closed with the balance carried down on the debit side. Decide which column of the trial balance should show it.

slides.heading: If the totals do not agree
slides.body_md: Use the **difference** as a clue before searching every entry.

rows: That balance may have been left out of the list
A debtor of ₹22,000 missing leaves the credit side higher by ₹22,000
Difference is exactly twice a balance
That balance may be on the wrong side
Carriage inwards of ₹9,000 entered as a credit makes the difference ₹18,000
Two digits may have been transposed
₹4,500 written as ₹5,400 gives a difference of ₹900
An error in adding or balancing an account
Re-add the columns and re-balance the ledgers

visual.alt: Table of four clues when the trial balance does not agree: a difference equal to one balance suggests an omitted balance, twice a balance suggests the wrong side, a multiple of nine suggests transposed digits, and a round difference suggests an adding or balancing error
visual.caption: If the totals do not agree

slides.narration: If the totals differ, look at the difference. If it equals one balance, that balance may have been left out. If it is twice a balance, the balance may be on the wrong side. If it divides by nine, digits may have been transposed. A round figure suggests an adding or balancing error.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: Each ledger balance is entered once, in the column of its nature
Assets, expenses, losses, purchases, sales return, opening stock, drawings
Capital, liabilities, incomes, sales, purchases return, provisions
Opening stock on the debit side; closing stock is not in the trial balance
Debit balances less the other credit balances
Journal, ledger, balances, then the trial balance

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: the balance method, the debit column, the credit column, the treatment of stock, finding a missing capital and preparing a trial balance from transactions

slides.narration: To sum up. In the balance method each ledger balance is entered once, on the side of its nature. Opening stock is a debit balance, closing stock is not in the trial balance, and a missing capital is the balancing figure. From transactions, prepare the journal, post, balance and list.

slides.heading: Exam tips

notes.title: Trial Balance — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Meaning and place of the trial balance
sections.body_md:
After transactions are journalised, posted to the ledger and every account is balanced, the accountant lists the balances in a **trial balance**.

- It is a **statement**, not an account, and has no folio.
- It is made **on a date**, usually the last day of the year.
- Debit balances are in one column and credit balances in the other; if the posting is accurate the totals **agree**.

The trial balance comes between the ledger and the final accounts.

key_terms.definition_md: A statement of the balances of all ledger accounts on a date, in a debit column and a credit column.
Preparing the trial balance from the closing balance of each account, entered once on its own side.

sections.heading: 2. Objectives and advantages
sections.body_md:
**Objectives:** to test the **arithmetical accuracy** of the books, to give a **summary of the ledger**, and to give the **base for the final accounts**.

**Advantages:** a quick check on posting; all balances in one place; easier final accounts; time saved in finding mistakes because a difference warns that something is wrong.

sections.heading: 3. What agreement shows, and the errors it hides
sections.body_md:
Agreement of the totals shows that **debits equal credits**. It does not show that the accounts are free from error. Four kinds of error leave the totals equal:

1. **Omission:** the transaction is not recorded at all.
2. **Principle:** an entry breaks an accounting principle, for example a capital item treated as an expense.
3. **Commission:** the wrong account is used, or the amount is wrong on both sides.
4. **Compensating errors:** two or more errors cancel each other.

Rectification of these errors is a separate chapter; here they are only named and recognised.

sections.heading: 5. The balance method: the side of each balance
sections.body_md:
Take the closing balance of each ledger account and place it on the side of its **nature**:

- **Debit:** assets, expenses, losses, purchases, sales return, opening stock, drawings.
- **Credit:** capital, liabilities (including bank overdraft), incomes, sales, purchases return, provisions.

Each account appears **once**. Add both columns and show that the totals are equal.

sections.heading: 6. Opening stock, closing stock and other items that cause trouble
sections.body_md:
**Opening stock** is a debit balance. **Closing stock** is found at the year end and is shown in the trading account and the balance sheet; if it is given as additional information it is **not** entered in the trial balance. Sales return is a **debit**, purchases return a **credit**, drawings a **debit**, bank overdraft and provisions are **credits**.

A balance carried down on the credit side of a ledger account is a **debit balance**, and the reverse, so read the nature, not the side of the c/d line.

sections.heading: 8. If the totals do not agree
sections.body_md:
First re-add the columns and re-check the balance of each account. Then use the **difference**: one balance left out equals the difference; a balance on the wrong side makes it **twice** that balance; transposed digits give a **multiple of nine**; a round figure suggests an adding mistake.

A difference is a warning to search. Equal totals are not proof of accuracy.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are usually split (ISC Accounts, Section A)**
- 1 mark: the side of a balance, or which error leaves the totals equal.
- 2 marks: the meaning of a trial balance, two objectives or advantages, or the side of four balances.
- 3 marks: a trial balance from about eight balances, three errors that do not affect the totals each with an example, or a missing capital.
- 5 marks: a full trial balance with sides to be decided, stock to be left out and capital to be found, or ledgers and a trial balance from transactions. Step marks go to each balance on the right side, the capital, the totals and the heading.

**Common mistakes**
- Calling the trial balance an account, or saying that agreement proves the books are correct.
- Entering closing stock given as additional information.
- Placing sales return on the credit side, drawings on the credit side, or a bank overdraft on the debit side.
- Treating a balance carried down on the credit side as a credit balance.
- Writing the trial balance without a date or without showing both totals.
- Leaving the working for a missing capital.

questions.stem_md: Hosur Hardware, an imagined firm, prepares a trial balance at the end of every month. The main objective of doing so is to

options.text_md: find the profit earned during the month
check the arithmetical accuracy of the posting and balancing of the ledger
find the market value of the assets
prove that no error has been committed in the books

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** check the arithmetical accuracy of the posting and balancing of the ledger. The statement tests whether total debits and total credits agree. It does not compute profit (that is the work of the final accounts), it has nothing to do with market values, and agreement can never prove that no error exists.

questions.stem_md: The trial balance of Nellore Pickles, an imagined firm, agrees at ₹8,40,000 on each side. Which one of these mistakes may still be present in its books?

options.text_md: A debit of ₹8,000 was posted to the ledger without its credit
A credit balance was written in the debit column of the trial balance
The balance of one account was carried down with a wrong amount
A credit purchase of goods was not entered in any book

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A credit purchase of goods was not entered in any book. A transaction left out altogether leaves debits and credits equal, so the totals cannot show it. Each of the other three mistakes would make the two columns differ.

questions.stem_md: A credit sale of goods for ₹22,500 to Ghatal Traders was not recorded in any book of Shimla Woollens, an imagined firm. This is an error of

options.text_md: omission
commission
principle
compensation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** omission. A transaction missing from the books altogether is an error of omission. Commission means a wrong account or amount, principle means a wrong class of account, and compensation needs two mistakes that cancel.

questions.stem_md: The trial balance of Chirala Seeds, an imagined firm, shows a debit total of ₹6,48,500 and a credit total of ₹6,39,500. Which single error explains the whole difference?

options.text_md: A debit entry of ₹9,000 was not posted to the ledger
A sale of ₹9,000 was left out of every book
A credit entry of ₹9,000 was not posted to the ledger
An expense of ₹4,500 was posted to the credit side instead of the debit side

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A credit entry of ₹9,000 was not posted to the ledger. The debit side is higher by ₹9,000, so a credit of that size is missing (or a debit is too much). A missing debit would lower the debit total, a complete omission changes neither total, and a wrong-side posting of ₹4,500 would leave the credit side higher.

questions.stem_md: Compensating errors in the books of Raiganj Tea Stall, an imagined firm, are errors which

options.text_md: arise from a transaction left out of the books altogether
arise when an item of capital nature is treated as an item of revenue
affect two or more accounts and cancel each other in their effect on the trial balance totals
arise when the right amount is entered in a wrong account of the same kind

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** affect two or more accounts and cancel each other in their effect on the trial balance totals. Cancelling effects are the mark of compensating errors. The other options describe omission, principle and commission respectively.

questions.stem_md: Whitefield Printers, an imagined firm, paid ₹14,500 for a new cutting machine and debited the amount to Repairs A/c. This is an error of

options.text_md: principle
omission
commission
compensation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** principle. A machine is a capital item but it was treated as a revenue expense, which breaks the principle of distinguishing capital from revenue. Nothing was omitted, the amount and sides are right, and no second error cancels it.

questions.stem_md: Jhansi Spices, an imagined firm, received a cheque of ₹9,800 from Mohan Beniwal and, by mistake, credited it to the account of Mohan Bhatnagar, another customer. The error is one of

options.text_md: principle
omission
compensation
commission

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** commission. The correct side and amount were used but the wrong personal account was chosen, which is an error of commission. The totals still agree, so the trial balance cannot show it.

questions.stem_md: Which one of the following is an advantage of a trial balance for Tonk Tractors, an imagined firm?

options.text_md: It proves that all the accounts are free from errors
All the ledger balances are available in one statement for preparing the final accounts
It discloses every error of omission and principle
It shows the profit of the firm without any further statement

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** All the ledger balances are available in one statement for preparing the final accounts. The one-statement summary is the real advantage. It cannot prove freedom from error, it does not reveal omission or principle errors, and profit comes only from the final accounts.

questions.stem_md: In the accounts of Sambalpur Sweets, an imagined firm, the trial balance is best described as

options.text_md: a statement of ledger balances prepared on a date to test the equality of debits and credits
an account kept in the ledger with a folio for every balance
a book of original entry for balances brought forward
a final account prepared at the end of the year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a statement of ledger balances prepared on a date to test the equality of debits and credits. It is a statement, and not an account. It has no folio, is not a book of original entry, and is prepared before the final accounts.

questions.stem_md: The owner of Dumka Dyes, an imagined firm, is told that the trial balance of the firm agrees and asks whether the books are therefore correct. The best reply is that

options.text_md: every transaction has been recorded in the right account
the posting is arithmetically accurate, but some kinds of error can still be present
no accounting principle has been broken in the books
the final accounts made from it will certainly be correct

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the posting is arithmetically accurate, but some kinds of error can still be present. Agreement is a test of equal debit and credit totals only. Completeness, correct accounts and correct principles are not tested, so the final accounts may still be affected.

questions.stem_md: What are compensating errors? Illustrate with an example from the books of Pilani Pencils, an imagined firm.

answer.model_answer_md:
Compensating errors are two or more mistakes whose effects on the totals cancel, so the trial balance agrees.

Example: the wages account is debited ₹3,000 too much, and the discount received account is credited ₹3,000 too much; the debit and credit totals rise equally.

questions.stem_md: Explain the trial balance under these heads: (a) meaning [1]; (b) three objectives [1]; (c) two advantages [1]; (d) two limitations, naming the errors it does not disclose [2].
questions.solution_md: One mark for each of (a), (b) and (c); two for (d).

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a) Meaning.** A trial balance is a statement of the debit and credit balances of all ledger accounts on a particular date.

**(b) Objectives.** (1) To test arithmetical accuracy. (2) To provide a summary of the ledger. (3) To provide the base for the final accounts.

**(c) Advantages.** (1) A quick check on posting. (2) A single statement makes the final accounts easier to prepare.

**(d) Limitations.** (1) Agreement is not proof of accuracy. (2) It does not disclose errors of omission, principle, commission and compensating errors, and it tests only the ledger.

questions.stem_md: Yercaud Coffee Traders, an imagined firm, finds these errors in its books: (i) a credit sale of ₹14,000 to Mysore Cafe was not entered in any book; (ii) machinery bought for ₹60,000 in cash was debited to Purchases A/c; (iii) a payment of ₹90,000 to Hosur Estates was debited to the account of Mysore Cafe; (iv) wages of ₹18,000 were debited to Wages A/c but Cash was not credited; (v) interest received of ₹6,000 was credited to Interest Received A/c as ₹9,000, the debit to Cash being correct. | (i) Credit sale of ₹14,000 not entered anywhere | Omission | Totals still agree: both the debit and the credit are missing |

questions.stem_md: The books of Nashik Nuts, an imagined firm, show opening stock of ₹36,000 and the stock at the end of the year is valued at ₹41,000. How will each be treated if a trial balance is prepared before the final accounts? State when closing stock does come into a trial balance.
questions.solution_md: One mark each for the opening stock, the closing stock, and the exception.

answer.model_answer_md:
The opening stock of ₹36,000 is a ledger balance and is a debit balance, so it is entered in the debit column.

The closing stock of ₹41,000 is not entered, because it is found only at the year end and is carried to the trading account and the balance sheet.

It appears in the trial balance only if it has already been adjusted in the books, for example by a closing entry, and the question says so.
